newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura indicted second time over racketeer scandal.
newsitem.headline: Nomura indicted second time over racketeer scandal.

text.p: Japan's top broker Nomura Securities was indicted for a second time on Wednesday, paving the way for financial authorities to take action on sanctions over the firm's involvement in a racketeering scandal.
Tokyo prosecutors said they indicted Nomura on charges of violating Japan's Securities and Exchange Law.

Also indicted was former president Hideo Sakamaki and former managing director Nobutaka Fujikura. The two are charged with conspiring with other Nomura officials to pay 320 million yen ($2.85 million) in cash to "sokaiya" corporate racketeer Ryuichi Koike around March 24, 1995.

The cash was paid in exchange for assurances from Koike that proceedings at a Nomura shareholders' meeting on June 29, 1995, would go smoothly, prosecutors said. The money was handed over in a reception room at Nomura's headquarters in Tokyo.
Sakamaki was arrested in late May and indicted on other charges in June for allegedly paying 49.73 million yen ($444,000) to Koike in 1995.
Nomura was also indicted in June for illegally compensating a company owned by Koike's brother for trading losses.

Sokaiya extort money from companies by threatening to disclose management misdeeds or disrupt annual shareholders meetings. Payoffs to the corporate extortionists have been illegal since 1983 but the practice has continued.
"We are accustomed to shocking revelations linked to the scandal. We will not be surprised with whatever happens," a Japanese government source said.
Soon after the indictment was unveiled, Nomura issued a statement saying that it would strive to avoid a recurrence of the scandal.
The scandal, which has led to the arrests of five Nomura officials, including Sakamaki, also involves one of Japan's top commercial banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB).
Prosecutors arrested 11 DKB officials, including former chairman Tadashi Okuda, on suspicion of approving loans to Ryuichi Koike.
Another former DKB chairman, Kuniji Miyazaki, killed himself late last month after he was questioned by prosecutors over his role in the scandal.
Following the indictments announced on Wednesday, authorities are expected to unveil the administrative penalties against the firm.
Market analysts have predicted that Nomura may be suspended from doing business for up to six months.
Such a move would not only severely undermine Nomura's bottom line but also dent its future status as the top brokerage in the "Big Bang" reforms in Japan.
The deregulation moves, meant to open up Japan's sheltered financial sector, have made authorities keen to take a tough stance against any wrongdoing.
"Depending on the extent of the penalties, Nomura may have to review its management strategy in the face of the Big Bang reforms," said a financial analyst at a European securities house.
Depending on the penalties, Nomura may need to consider an alliance to meet growing competition as investors' confidence in Nomura has deteriorated sharply, he said.
The SESC is expected to make its recommendations on penalties to the Finance Ministry, which has the final say, later this week or early next week, financial sources said.
